newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Auction may help shaky market.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Auction may help shaky market.

text.p: Gilts will have a tough time shaking off the blues plaguing other bond markets this week but a 10-year auction may provide some cheer, analysts said.
The sale of 2.5 billion stg of 10-year gilts on Wednesday provides the week's key litmus test for the market. On the data front, only trade and consumer credit figures are on offer.

"My gut feeling is that the auction should go quite well," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "It's a smaller amount than people expected and is in a reasonable area of the curve to attract demand."
So far this financial year the Bank of England has been in the habit of auctioning 3.0 billion stg of stock each month.

Brian Hilliard, senior international economist at Societe Generale, said the poor tone in the gilt market could hit the auction. "But after the auction it will be sufficiently cheap to represent good value on the curve," he said in a client note.
He advised buying the 10-year gilt after the auction and selling the 8.0 percent gilts due 2021. The Bank of England is expected to sell that stock in September.
But whatever happens with Wednesday's tender, gilts will have difficulty pushing ahead if U.S. Treasuries spiral lower.
The September U.S. T-bond future dropped nearly a point on Monday, pushing Bunds lower while gilts were untraded as Britain holidayed.

On Tuesday, gilts predictably caught the cold that tends to follow a U.S. sneeze. The September future fell about a half-point in early trade before bouncing from exactly 107-00. That remains a key level for the week, dealers said.
In data terms, Wednesday's non-EU trade figures for July and for the whole world for June are unlikely to set the market alight.
"Trade data...almost never affect bonds," Hilliard said.
That leaves only July consumer credit on Friday for the market to get its teeth into. A Reuter poll of economists forecasts credit up 800 million stg in July. In June credit rose by just 636 million.
Hilliard said the figure, if it matched forecasts, would be a minor negative for gilts. "In general, the tone looks poor and gilt prices should drift lower."
Coleman agreed, seeing little short-term scope for outperformance by the UK market.
The gilt/Bund spread pushed in to 160 basis points on Monday but soon widened again, to 166, on Tuesday.
"The negative tone in other markets will swamp gilts for now," Coleman said. "Short-term, no further outperformance, but ultimately I would still look for 155, maybe 150."

With hopes rising of a base rate cut following the September 4 monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, analysts at PaineWebber International forecast curve steepening.

"Data over the past few weeks have kept the window of opportunity open for the Chancellor to cut rates, should he wish to," they said in a client note. "We think he will, on political grounds, and target the September 4 meeting."
